\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{नीचः} (nīcaḥ)}{नीचः (nīcaḥ)}]{\sk{नीचः} (nīcaḥ) — low}

\label{lesson:SA-C133-nicah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for full, then the Sanskrit for empty.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{नीचः}}
\textbf{\sk{नीचः}} — \emph{nīcaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}low\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{nīca} is built from \emph{ni} \textquotedblleft{}down\textquotedblright{} and the root √añc \textquotedblleft{}bend, turn\textquotedblright{} (MW; CDIAL 7540): \textquotedblleft{}turned downward\textquotedblright{}, so \textquotedblleft{}low\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Hindi and Punjabi \emph{nīcā} \textquotedblleft{}low\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 7540).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nīcaḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nīcaḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for full, then the Sanskrit for empty, then say \emph{nīcaḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{उन्नतः} (unnataḥ)}{उन्नतः (unnataḥ)}]{\sk{उन्नतः} (unnataḥ) — high, tall}

\label{lesson:SA-C133-unnatah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for empty, then the Sanskrit for low.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{उन्नतः}}
\textbf{\sk{उन्नतः}} — \emph{unnataḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}high, tall\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{unnata} is the past participle of \emph{ud-√nam} \textquotedblleft{}bend upward, rise\textquotedblright{}, the root √nam \textquotedblleft{}bend, bow\textquotedblright{} with \emph{ud} \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{} (MW; CDIAL 2099): \textquotedblleft{}raised, high, tall\textquotedblright{}. It is the same root as \emph{namas} in \emph{namaste}, the greeting you already know.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{unnataḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{unnataḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for empty, then the Sanskrit for low, then say \emph{unnataḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{उड्डयते} (uḍḍayate)}{उड्डयते (uḍḍayate)}]{\sk{उड्डयते} (uḍḍayate) — flies}

\label{lesson:SA-C133-uddayate}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for low, then the Sanskrit for high.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{उड्डयते}}
\textbf{\sk{उड्डयते}} — \emph{uḍḍayate} — \textquotedblleft{}flies\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{uḍḍayate} comes from \emph{ud-√ḍī} \textquotedblleft{}fly up, soar\textquotedblright{}, the root √ḍī \textquotedblleft{}fly\textquotedblright{} with \emph{ud} \textquotedblleft{}up\textquotedblright{} (MW; CDIAL 1697). It lives on as Hindi \emph{uṛnā} and Marathi \emph{uḍṇe} \textquotedblleft{}to fly\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 1697).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तरति} (tarati)}{तरति (tarati)}]{\sk{तरति} (tarati) — swims, crosses}

\label{lesson:SA-C133-tarati}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for high, then the Sanskrit for flies.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तरति}}
\textbf{\sk{तरति}} — \emph{tarati} — \textquotedblleft{}swims, crosses\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tarati} comes from the root √tṝ \textquotedblleft{}cross over\textquotedblright{}, and then \textquotedblleft{}float, swim\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5702). The root is inherited from Indo-European (EtymDB), and MW sets it beside Latin \emph{trans} \textquotedblleft{}across\textquotedblright{} and \emph{terminus} \textquotedblleft{}boundary\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Hindi \emph{tarnā} \textquotedblleft{}to cross\textquotedblright{} and Punjabi \emph{tarnā} \textquotedblleft{}to swim\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5702).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कूर्दति} (kūrdati)}{कूर्दति (kūrdati)}]{\sk{कूर्दति} (kūrdati) — jumps}

\label{lesson:SA-C133-kurdati}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for flies, then the Sanskrit for swims.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कूर्दति}}
\textbf{\sk{कूर्दति}} — \emph{kūrdati} — \textquotedblleft{}jumps\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kūrdati} \textquotedblleft{}leaps, jumps\textquotedblright{} is probably borrowed from Dravidian: CDIAL 3412, after Burrow, compares a Dravidian verb for springing. It lives on as Hindi \emph{kūdnā} \textquotedblleft{}to jump\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3412).
\end{cousinweb}
